name: Ragavendra
definition: Ragavendra is a composite portrait of a Vokkaliga electrical contractor and small farmer in Magadi taluk, Ramanagara district, navigating the economic pressures of rural electrification work, dry-land cultivation and the rising costs of raising a family in the semi-rural belt between Bengaluru and Mysuru. His household sits at the intersection of Old Mysuru's agrarian identity and the spreading influence of Bengaluru's urban economy, where local livelihoods depend on both the land and the construction boom driven by the capital's expansion.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Ragavendra runs a small electrical contracting business in Magadi taluk, wiring houses, installing pump-sets and handling contracts for village streetlights and anganwadi buildings. He bids for panchayat tenders and private jobs in Magadi town and surrounding villages, often travelling on his two-wheeler to sites within a twenty-kilometre radius. His income varies sharply month to month—a good quarter brings in forty to fifty thousand rupees, while lean periods yield half that or less, depending on rainfall, construction activity and payment delays from government schemes. He also cultivates four acres of ancestral dry land near his village, growing ragi and groundnut. The farm relies on bore-well water; two successive dry years have forced him to leave one acre fallow. He hires labourers at peak times and works the land himself when contracts are slow. The twin pressures of fluctuating contract income and uncertain monsoons mean he carefully times expenses, postponing equipment purchases and relying on a small overdraft facility at the district co-operative bank. Fuel costs for travel and rising copper-wire prices squeeze his margins, and clients—both private and panchayat—often delay payment by months. The work keeps him occupied six days a week; Sundays he spends on the farm or catching up on paperwork and quotations.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Ragavendra lives in a pucca house in a village six kilometres from Magadi town with his wife Suma, their two children—a daughter aged thirteen and a son aged nine—and his widowed mother, who is seventy. Suma manages the household and helps with farm labour during sowing and harvest; she also rears a small dairy cow and sells the milk to the village co-operative collector, adding three to four thousand rupees a month to the family budget. His mother, though frail, cooks and looks after the children when Suma is at the farm. Ragavendra's younger brother migrated to Bengaluru a decade ago and works in a private security firm; they meet only during festivals and family functions. Gender roles in the household follow a traditional division: Suma handles all cooking, childcare and the dairy work, while Ragavendra manages the contracting business and farm decisions. The family shares meals together in the evenings when Ragavendra is home; dinner conversation often turns to the children's schooling and the cost of private tuition. His marriage was arranged by the families seventeen years ago, and extended kin—mostly Vokkaliga relatives in Magadi and Ramanagara taluks—gather for life-cycle ceremonies and the annual Karaga procession in the nearby temple.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Ragavendra completed his SSLC at the government high school in Magadi town, travelling by KSRTC bus as a teenager; he did not continue to PUC, instead learning electrical work as an apprentice under a local contractor. He values education and is determined that his children will study further than he did. His daughter attends a private Kannada-medium school in Magadi town, travelling daily by the Shakti free bus; the school charges five thousand rupees a year in fees, and he pays an additional two thousand for English and maths tuition on weekends. His son studies at the same school in fourth standard. Ragavendra hopes his daughter will complete at least a degree—perhaps B.Com or BA—and find office work or a government job, something he sees as more secure than contracting. The family worries about the cost of PUC and degree college later: private colleges in Ramanagara or Bengaluru charge fees he will struggle to afford without a loan. His daughter is a steady student, ranking in the top quarter of her class; his son is less interested in schoolwork and prefers playing cricket in the village. Ragavendra has heard of scholarship schemes for rural children but has not yet applied. The Shakti bus pass has made a tangible difference—his daughter no longer walks the six kilometres, and Suma no longer worries about her safety on the road.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: The family depends on the Magadi taluk hospital for outpatient care and the government PHC in their village for vaccinations and minor ailments. Ragavendra's mother has diabetes and high blood pressure; she receives subsidised medicines under the Arogya Karnataka scheme, but the taluk hospital often runs short of stock, forcing the family to buy from private pharmacies in Magadi town at higher cost. Two years ago Ragavendra fell from a ladder at a worksite and fractured his wrist; he went to a private orthopaedic clinic in Ramanagara town and paid fifteen thousand rupees out of pocket—the family borrowed from a relative to cover it. His wife and children are generally healthy, though his daughter has had recurrent anaemia, flagged at a school health camp. The doctor advised iron supplements and dietary changes; Suma has added more greens and ragi mudde to meals, and the girl's haemoglobin has improved. Ragavendra does not smoke but drinks occasionally with friends at village functions. The household worries most about major illness or injury—they have no private health insurance, and hospitalisation would mean distress borrowing or selling livestock. The nearest private hospital with an ICU is in Ramanagara town, twenty-five kilometres away, an hour's drive that feels longer in an emergency.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Ragavendra's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, the dominant cultivating caste in Ramanagara and across the Old Mysuru region. Caste shapes social networks: most of his contracting contacts, lending relationships and labour arrangements run through Vokkaliga networks in Magadi taluk. The family observes festivals tied to the agricultural calendar—Ugadi, Sankranti and Deepavali—and makes an annual pilgrimage to the Cheluvanarayana Swamy temple in Melukote during the Vairamudi festival, a major Vokkaliga religious gathering. His mother is devout, visiting the village Hanuman temple every morning and conducting monthly pujas at home. Ragavendra is less regular in temple-going but participates in village temple festivals and contributes to the temple trust. The village has a small Muslim minority; relations are cordial, and Muslim households contract Ragavendra for electrical work without hesitation. Caste tensions are muted in daily life, though Scheduled Caste families in the village live in a separate street, and inter-dining is rare. Ragavendra's social circle comprises other Vokkaliga contractors, traders and farmers; they gather at a local tea shop in the evenings to discuss contracts, farm prices and politics. Community support is strong: when his mother was hospitalised, neighbours and relatives contributed cash and visited daily.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: The Shakti scheme has directly benefited his daughter's schooling, and the Gruha Jyoti subsidy saves the household a few hundred rupees monthly on electricity bills, though he is sceptical about how long the schemes will last. He has dealt with the gram panchayat for streetlight contracts and ration-card updates; officials are accessible but payment for completed panchayat work is slow, often six months in arrears. He has not applied for MGNREGA work—contractors like him are ineligible—but hires MGNREGA labourers at the mandated wage when their hundred days are exhausted. He holds a Bhoomi land record and an Aadhar-linked bank account; digitisation has made land transactions easier, though he once had to visit the taluk office three times to correct an error in his survey number. Ragavendra is frustrated by the lack of better rural roads and reliable three-phase power supply, which affects both his contracting equipment and farm pump-sets. He sees government as distant—responding slowly to local needs—but essential for schooling, health and farm subsidies. He has never attended a gram sabha but knows the local Congress MLA by sight and reputation.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Ragavendra is proud of his Vokkaliga heritage and of belonging to the Old Mysuru region, which he sees as the cultural and administrative heart of Karnataka, home to Mysuru's Dasara and the state's legacy. He worries most about money—whether contract payments will come on time, whether the bore-well will yield water next summer, whether he can afford his children's college fees without distress borrowing. He blames the erratic monsoon and what he calls government apathy for the struggles of small farmers; he believes the Cauvery water is taken for granted and that Ramanagara's dry-land farmers get less attention than the canal-irrigated belt in Mandya. He is proud that his daughter is studying and determined that she will not have to depend on farm income. He resents the pressure from Bengaluru's expansion—land prices have risen sharply, and labour is harder to find as workers leave for city construction jobs—but he also sees opportunity in the building boom and the new Bengaluru-Mysuru Expressway, which has brought more contracts his way. He wants better rural infrastructure—paved roads, reliable power, a taluk hospital with specialists—and he is hopeful that the Congress guarantees signal a government more responsive to ordinary families. He sees himself as a small-time entrepreneur and a farmer, juggling two livelihoods, trying to lift his children into salaried security.
